title: Crécy and Agincourt
objective: After this level you can explain how English longbows won at Crécy and Agincourt.
summary: At Crécy (1346) longbows outshot crossbows and broke repeated charges; at Agincourt (1415) archers behind stakes beat the French across a muddy field. Army sizes are debated.

cards.headline: Two famous English wins. The bows are certain. The head counts are not.
cards.body: At Crécy and Agincourt, English archers beat bigger French armies during the Hundred Years’ War. How much bigger? Historians still argue, so you’ll get ranges, not a single number.

cards.headline: Crécy, 1346
cards.body: On 26 August 1346, Edward III’s army met the French at Crécy. Italian crossbowmen opened the French attack and were routed by English archers, whose longbows could shoot about three times as fast. Then came the French charges, some 15 or 16 of them, each cut down by arrows. Three arrows for every bolt is a hard trade to win.

cards.headline: Agincourt, 1415
cards.body: On 25 October 1415, Henry V’s army stood on a recently ploughed field squeezed between woods. The archers had driven sharpened stakes into the ground in front of them. The French had to advance through mud, straight into the arrows. The battle probably lasted no more than three hours. The field did half the fighting.

mascot.line: Mud, stakes and a narrow field: sometimes the ground picks the winner before anyone draws a bow.

cards.headline: How many? It depends who counts

items.label: Agincourt
points: Traditional: about 6,000 English against 20,000 to 30,000 French
Anne Curry: about 8,500 English against around 12,000 French

cards.headline: Counting with the paperwork
cards.body: How do you count an army centuries later? Historian Anne Curry worked through the muster rolls and financial records, the payroll of the Agincourt campaign. She argues the vast French army once claimed couldn’t even have fitted on the battlefield. Still outnumbered, then, but not hopelessly: a hard win built on arrows and mud.

cards.headline: Crécy and Agincourt: known
learned: Agincourt, 1415: stakes, a narrow field and mud
Army sizes are debated, so historians give ranges
Anne Curry counted from campaign records

questions.prompt: At Crécy in 1346, what gave English longbowmen the edge over the crossbowmen?

options.label: Their arrows were tipped with poison
They could shoot about three times as fast
They shot from inside a walled castle
They had cannon firing behind them
options.rationale: The story here is the longbow.

questions.explanation: English longbows could shoot about three times as fast as crossbows, and the crossbowmen were routed.

questions.prompt: Why do historians give ranges for the size of the armies at Agincourt?

options.label: No one wrote anything at all down about the campaign
options.rationale: Muster rolls and financial records survive.

options.label: Estimates differ, and records suggest fewer French than once claimed
Both armies were exactly the same size, so no one bothered
options.rationale: The French still outnumbered the English.

options.label: The battle lasted too many days for anyone to count
options.rationale: It probably lasted under three hours.

questions.explanation: Traditional estimates say about 6,000 against 20,000 to 30,000; Anne Curry’s records suggest about 8,500 against around 12,000.

questions.prompt: Despite winning at Crécy and Agincourt, how did the Hundred Years’ War end for England?

options.label: It won the French crown for its kings for good
options.rationale: England lost nearly everything in France.

options.label: It kept all of Gascony and most of Normandy
It gained Paris by a peace treaty
It lost all its French lands except Calais

questions.explanation: Great battles aside, by 1453 England had lost all its lands in France except Calais.
